title: Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties
bodyText: Federal law adds a notice rule for some rentals, on top of your state's notices. Under the CARES Act, if the property has a federally backed mortgage, or takes part in a covered federal housing program or the rural housing voucher program, you may not require the tenant to vacate until 30 days after you give a notice to vacate (15 U.S.C. § 9058(c)). For a property of one to four units, a federally backed mortgage includes a loan made, insured, guaranteed or assisted by a federal agency (for example FHA, VA or USDA loans) and a loan bought or securitized by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac (15 U.S.C. § 9058(a)(4)); larger properties have a matching multifamily definition. The same law's temporary eviction moratorium ended in 2020, but the 30-day notice section has no end date. Courts disagree about whether it still applies, and whether it reaches only evictions for nonpayment; this library has not reviewed those decisions. If your loan may be federally backed (your servicer can tell you), the safe course is to give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate before filing, or your state's longer notice where it is longer. Some state court rules also ask for a statement about it when you file.

title: Federal Tenant Protections After Foreclosure
bodyText: Federal law protects tenants when a rental home is foreclosed. Under the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, whoever takes title through the foreclosure (often the lender) takes it subject to the rights of any bona fide tenant. A tenant whose lease was signed before the notice of foreclosure may stay until the lease ends, and a month-to-month tenant, or one with no written lease, must get at least 90 days' notice to vacate. The one exception: if the new owner sells the unit to a buyer who will live in it as a primary residence, the lease may end on the date of that sale, but the tenant still gets the 90 days' notice. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant is not the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, the deal was at arm's length, and the rent is not substantially below fair market rent (unless a government subsidy reduces it). For this law, the notice of foreclosure is the date title transfers to the new owner. This matters to you two ways: if your property is foreclosed, your tenants keep these rights against the new owner; and if you take title to a home through a foreclosure with tenants in it, you must honor them. State or local law that gives tenants more time or protection still applies, as do the rules for ending a subsidized tenancy.

title: Federal Notice When a Screening Report Leads to a Denial
bodyText: If you turn an applicant down because of something in a credit report, tenant-screening report or background check from a screening company, even in part, federal law requires you to tell the applicant. The same applies to any other decision against the applicant based on the report, such as requiring a larger deposit, a cosigner or higher rent. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, you must give notice of the decision (it may be oral, but written is the safe course; keep a copy) that includes: the name, address and phone number of the company that supplied the report (and its toll-free number if it is a nationwide agency); a statement that the company did not make the decision and can't explain why it was made; the applicant's right to a free copy of the report from that company within 60 days; and the right to dispute inaccurate or incomplete information with the company. If you used a credit score, you must also disclose the score and the related facts the Act lists. A landlord who willfully fails to comply can owe actual damages or statutory damages of $100 to $1,000, plus punitive damages and the applicant's attorney fees; a negligent failure can cost actual damages and attorney fees. Having reasonable procedures to comply, such as always sending the notice, is a defense. Many screening companies supply a ready-made adverse-action letter. Your state may add its own screening rules; see this state's other screening rows.

title: Federal Rule on Disposing of Screening Reports
bodyText: If you keep a credit report, tenant-screening report or background check from a screening company, or any record taken from one (such as notes that copy an applicant's credit details), federal law says how you must get rid of it. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act's disposal rule, anyone who keeps this information for a business purpose, including a landlord who screens applicants, must take reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access to or use of it when disposing of it. Disposal includes throwing records away or abandoning them, and selling, donating or giving away a computer, phone or drive that holds them. The rule gives examples of reasonable measures: burning, pulverizing or shredding paper so it can't practicably be read or reconstructed; destroying or erasing electronic files and devices the same way; or hiring a record-destruction company after checking it out (for example its references, an independent audit of its operations or a trade certification) and monitoring its work. The rule covers records about approved applicants and tenants as well as denied ones, but not information that identifies no one, such as totals. It doesn't say how long to keep a report or require you to destroy one; another law may require you to keep records for a period, and this rule doesn't change that. The Federal Trade Commission enforces it. Your state may add its own rules on tenant records and personal information; see this state's other records rows.

title: Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease
bodyText: If you rent to a tenant with a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8), you sign a housing assistance payments (HAP) contract with the local public housing agency, and federal rules change how your lease works. HUD's tenancy addendum must be added to your lease word for word; the tenant can enforce it against you, and it controls over anything in the lease that conflicts with it. The lease must be in writing and state the owner and tenant, the unit, the term, the monthly rent to owner, and which utilities and appliances you and the family each supply. During the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation (including not paying the family's share of the rent), a violation of law tied to the tenant's use of the home, or other good cause. During the initial term, other good cause must be something the family did or failed to do, so not, for example, a sale, a renovation, moving in yourself or wanting higher rent. You may not end the tenancy because the housing agency didn't pay its share, and the family owes only its own share. You must give the tenant a written notice stating the grounds, at or before the start of an eviction, give the agency a copy of any eviction notice, and evict only through court. Lease changes must be in writing with a copy to the agency right away; a change to the term or to who supplies utilities or appliances needs the agency's approval and a new HAP contract; and you must tell the agency of a rent change at least 60 days before it takes effect. Your state's eviction law still applies on top of these rules.

title: Federal Assistance-Animal Enforcement Change (HUD, 2025-2026)
bodyText: Federal news about emotional support animals is easy to misread. HUD withdrew its assistance-animal guidance (FHEO Notice 2013-01 and FHEO-2020-01) effective September 17, 2025 (91 Fed. Reg. 17291). Then, in an enforcement memorandum dated May 22, 2026, HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity said it will find reasonable cause and recommend Fair Housing Act charges only for animals trained to provide disability-related assistance, and that it no longer expects landlords to treat untrained emotional support animals the same way. Here is what that does not change. The Fair Housing Act and HUD's regulation requiring reasonable accommodations in rules and policies (24 C.F.R. § 100.204) have not changed. The memo itself says it does not affect a tenant's right to sue in federal or state court, which the Act allows within two years (42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A)), and it does not address complaints under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act or the Americans with Disabilities Act, which can reach federally assisted and public housing. Your state's own fair housing or disability law, where it has one, is untouched by a federal enforcement memo. HUD says it intends to change its regulations through notice-and-comment rulemaking. Until a new rule is final, this library's assistance-animal clause keeps treating an animal a tenant or occupant needs for a disability, trained or not, as an accommodation rather than a pet. That gives more than HUD will now enforce, and it is lawful. If you want a narrower policy, you can write your own clause, but read your state's assistance-animal rows first, since some states protect emotional support animals by statute.

title: Federal Eviction Protections for Servicemembers
bodyText: Federal law adds protections when a tenant is in military service. Under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, you may not evict a servicemember, or a servicemember's dependents, during military service from a home they occupy or intend to occupy primarily as a residence, where the monthly rent is no more than a limit adjusted each year, except by court order. For 2026 the limit is $10,542.60 a month (the Defense Department's notice of March 10, 2026); check the current year's figure. Knowingly evicting, or trying to evict, without a court order is a federal crime. In an eviction case, the court may on its own, and must if the servicemember asks and military service materially affects their ability to pay the rent, stay the case for 90 days (or a longer or shorter period the court finds fair) or adjust the lease obligation. Separately, in any lawsuit in which the tenant doesn't appear, including an eviction or a suit for unpaid rent, the court must have you file an affidavit before it enters judgment, stating whether or not the tenant is in military service with the facts that support it, or that you can't determine it; a knowingly false affidavit is a federal crime. If the tenant is in military service, the court can't enter judgment until it appoints a lawyer for them. And anyone holding a lien on a servicemember's property, including a lien for storing it, may not enforce it during military service or for 90 days after without a court order, so belongings a servicemember leaves behind need care. Your state's eviction and abandoned-property rules still apply on top of these; a servicemember's right to end a lease early is covered separately.

title: Federal Bankruptcy Stay and Evictions
bodyText: When a tenant files for bankruptcy, federal law automatically stops most collection and eviction steps against them (the automatic stay). It bars, among other things, starting or continuing a court case against the tenant that was or could have been started before the filing, any act to get possession of property of the bankruptcy estate, and any act to collect a claim that arose before the filing. A tenant hurt by a willful violation of the stay recovers actual damages, including costs and attorney's fees, and may recover punitive damages. Two exceptions apply to a tenant living in the home. First, if you got a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, you may continue the eviction, unless the tenant files with the petition, and serves on you, a certification under penalty of perjury that your state's law would let them cure the whole money default after the judgment, and deposits with the court clerk the rent that comes due in the 30 days after filing. The stay then lasts 30 days, and longer only if the tenant certifies within those 30 days that the whole default is cured. You may object to either certification, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. Second, an eviction based on endangering the property or on illegal drug use on it may go forward 15 days after you file with the court, and serve on the tenant, a certification under penalty of perjury that the eviction has been filed, or that in the past 30 days the tenant endangered the property or illegally used, or allowed the use of, a controlled substance there, unless the tenant objects and shows the court the situation didn't exist or has been remedied. In any other case, ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay before taking any step, and talk to a lawyer first: the rules are technical and the damages are real.

title: Who the Federal Fair Housing Act Covers
bodyText: The federal Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in renting a home because of race, color, religion, sex, disability (the Act says 'handicap'), familial status or national origin. Familial status means having a child under 18 living with a parent or legal custodian (or someone they designate in writing), and it also protects someone who is pregnant or getting custody of a child. The Act covers almost every rental, with two narrow exemptions. One is a single-family house rented by a private individual owner who owns no more than three single-family houses at a time, and only if it's rented without any real estate broker or agent, or anyone in the business of renting homes, and without a discriminatory advertisement. The other is a building with living quarters for no more than four families living independently, where the owner lives in one of them. The first is written for a 'private individual owner', so an owner renting through a company shouldn't count on it. Even an exempt owner may not make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination on any of these grounds, such as a listing that says 'adults only'. A separate federal law gives all citizens the same right to lease property as white citizens, with no exemption for small owners. The Act doesn't limit reasonable local, state or federal limits on how many people may live in a dwelling, and its familial-status rules don't apply to qualifying housing for older persons. Your state's fair housing law may cover more grounds and more owners, and still applies.

title: Federal Rules on Harassment and Interference
bodyText: Federal fair housing law bars harassing tenants and applicants because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability. HUD's rule names two kinds. Quid pro quo harassment is an unwelcome request or demand (for example, for sex) made a condition of renting, of the lease's terms, or of services such as repairs, and it counts even if the person goes along with it. Hostile environment harassment is unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to interfere with renting the home or using and enjoying it, judged from the view of a reasonable person in the victim's position; no psychological or physical harm has to be shown. A single incident can be enough if it is severe enough. You are liable for your own conduct; for failing to act promptly to correct and end discrimination by your employee or agent when you knew or should have known of it; and for failing to act promptly to correct and end discrimination by someone else, such as another tenant, when you knew or should have known of it and had the power to correct it. The steps you take may not penalize or harm the person harassed, for example by evicting them. You are also liable for your agent's or employee's discrimination even if you didn't know of it. Separately, the Act makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights, or for helping someone else exercise them, which reaches retaliation against a tenant who complains of discrimination. Your state's law may add more.

title: Federal Accessible Design Rules for Newer Buildings
bodyText: The Fair Housing Act sets accessibility requirements for multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991. They cover every unit in a building of 4 or more units that has an elevator, and the ground-floor units in other buildings of 4 or more units. Those buildings had to be designed and built so that the public and common areas are readily accessible to and usable by people with disabilities, every door into and within the units is wide enough for a wheelchair, and each covered unit has an accessible route into and through it; light switches, outlets, thermostats and other controls in accessible places; reinforced bathroom walls so grab bars can be added later; and kitchens and bathrooms a wheelchair user can move around in. Meeting the ANSI A117.1 accessibility standard satisfies the in-unit features. The requirement is stated as a duty of design and construction, so it matters most when you build, convert or buy such a building: ask whether it was built to these rules. Single-family houses and buildings of 3 or fewer units are not covered. Separately, any tenant with a disability may make reasonable modifications, and ask for reasonable accommodations, in any covered rental (see the disability rows). Your state or city building code may require more.

title: Federal Debt Collection Law and Who It Covers
bodyText: The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act governs debt collectors, not a landlord collecting its own rent in its own name. It covers consumer debts, those for personal, family or household purposes, which include a tenant's rent and charges for a home. A debt collector is anyone in a business whose principal purpose is collecting debts, or who regularly collects debts owed to someone else. It doesn't include your own officers or employees collecting in your name, or a person collecting a debt that was not in default when they got it, so a property manager who collects rent as it comes due is generally outside it. But a manager or company that takes over an account only after it is past due, or a collection agency or anyone else you hire who regularly collects debts for others, may be a debt collector and must follow the Act's rules on communications, validation notices and unfair practices. And if you collect your own debts under any name other than your own that suggests a third party is collecting, you become a debt collector yourself. Your state's collection laws may reach landlords collecting their own debts, and still apply.

title: Federal Asbestos Rules for Renovating Larger Buildings
bodyText: Federal clean-air rules for asbestos apply to demolishing or renovating a residential building with five or more dwelling units; residential buildings with four or fewer units are excluded. Before demolishing or renovating any part of such a building, the owner or operator must have the affected part thoroughly inspected for asbestos. If the work will disturb at least 260 linear feet of regulated asbestos-containing material on pipes, 160 square feet on other parts of the building, or 35 cubic feet where it couldn't be measured, the owner or operator must give the EPA (or the state or local agency the EPA has delegated the program to) written notice at least 10 working days before the work begins, update it if the amount changes by at least 20 percent, and follow the rules' handling and disposal practices. Demolishing such a building needs the 10-working-day notice even if there is less asbestos than that, or none. Workers who remove asbestos are also covered by federal workplace-safety rules. Your state may license asbestos inspectors and contractors and add rules of its own.

title: Federal Rule on Satellite Dishes and Antennas
bodyText: An FCC rule limits what a lease may say about satellite dishes and antennas. It protects a tenant's satellite dish one meter (about 39 inches) or less across, a similar-sized antenna for wireless TV or fixed wireless internet, a TV broadcast antenna, and a mast supporting one, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control under the lease, such as a private balcony or patio. A lease provision that unreasonably delays or prevents installing, maintaining or using one, unreasonably increases its cost, or keeps the tenant from getting an acceptable-quality signal is prohibited, unless it is needed for a clearly defined, legitimate safety objective or to preserve a historic property listed on or eligible for the National Register, and is no more burdensome than necessary. Any fee you charge must be reasonable. The rule doesn't reach common areas or other parts of the property the tenant doesn't have exclusive use of, such as a shared roof, so you may keep tenants from installing there.

title: Federal Voucher Rules on Repairs and Rent
bodyText: If you rent to a tenant with a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8), federal rules also govern repairs and what you may charge. You must keep the unit up to the program's housing quality standards. Once the housing agency or inspector notifies you in writing of a deficiency, you must fix a life-threatening one within 24 hours and any other within 30 calendar days (or a reasonable extension the agency approves). The agency may withhold its payments from written notice and pays them back if you make the repairs in time; if you don't, it must abate (stop) its payments, including the withheld amounts, and will end your contract for the unit if it isn't fixed within 60 days or a longer period the agency sets. You may not end the tenancy because the agency withheld or stopped its payments, and failing to maintain the unit is a breach of your contract with the agency. If the tenant, a household member or guest caused the deficiency (beyond ordinary use), the agency may waive your duty to fix it. The rent to owner must be reasonable compared with similar unassisted units, as the agency decides, and the agency rechecks it before any increase. You may not demand or accept from the tenant more than the rent to owner minus the agency's payment, must return any excess right away, and the tenant isn't responsible for the agency's share. You may not charge the tenant extra for items customarily included in rent locally, or provided at no extra cost to unsubsidized tenants in the building, and the lease may not require the tenant to pay for meals or supportive services. The tenancy rules and HUD's tenancy addendum are covered separately.

title: Federal Duties When You Report Rent to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: If you report a tenant's rent payments, or an unpaid balance, to a credit bureau, directly or through a rent-reporting service that reports in your name, federal law makes you a 'furnisher' with duties of your own under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. You may not report information you know, or have reasonable cause to believe, is inaccurate. If you regularly report and learn that something you reported is incomplete or inaccurate, you must promptly send the bureau the correction and stop reporting the wrong information. If a tenant disputes an item with you, you may not report it again without saying it is disputed. When you report an account placed for collection, charged off or similar, you must tell the bureau, within 90 days, the month and year the delinquency began. When a credit bureau forwards a tenant's dispute to you, you must investigate, review what the bureau sends, report the results to it, and correct, delete or block an item that is inaccurate, incomplete or can't be verified, all within the bureau's own deadline (generally 30 days after the bureau receives the dispute, sometimes 45); a tenant can sue you for failing at this step. You must also have reasonable written policies and procedures for the accuracy and integrity of what you report, suited to the size of your operation and reviewed periodically, and reasonably investigate most disputes a tenant sends you directly at the address you give for them or that appears on the credit report (or any business address, if you give none). If a collection agency you hire does the reporting, these duties are mainly the agency's; check what your contract with it says. Your state may have its own rent-reporting rules, and they still apply.

title: No Subordination Clause in the Library
bodyText: The library does not offer a subordination clause, one that makes your lease rank below a mortgage on the property. Lenders and commercial leases use them so that a lease cannot stand in the way of a foreclosure. In a residential tenancy it adds little: if the property is foreclosed, a bona fide tenant's main protection against the new owner comes from the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act (see `edu-ptfa-foreclosure-tenants`). If your lender requires a subordination clause, you can add your own; check your state's law first.
